I'll do my best to explain what is happening here, as I see it.

There's a reason Paul Graham wrote Hackers and Painters and not Hackers and Assembly Line Workers.

Many people long to be craftsmen and to have an understanding of their place in the world and within the social hierarchy.

These folks want to perfect some art or craft, to be the best, or to be skillful, to "create" and find joy in creation, and they pursue a level of purity in the art. Totally human, completely normal, and part of what has led to our success and advancement as a species. Think about your open-source maintainer, or the gal who has Ruby on Rails stickers plastered on their laptop, or maybe you yourself as you try to get excited about the super boring details about the latest release of some open-source package you want to be the expert in (why?). They want to be "hackers" and "painters"!

The problem is that the pursuit of this particular craft (software development) falls into the realm of Science and Industry. Engineering, code, electronics, machines, experiments - all of these things and more are part of those two fields and those two fields by definition require and improve upon existing technology or understanding and as such they are fields which change often, cause some skills to become obsolete without remorse, and they do so at a fast pace.

The software engineer who believes in their craft and their expertise in JavaScript is finding that Science and Industry no longer value that craft and expertise - so that person's place in the world is directly under threat, including their income in many cases. It causes a range of emotional reactions.

You can see how this manifests with many software engineers going on to do silly things like move to Japan and live on a mountain top to write code in peace, or start a Substack newsletter that nobody ever reads, or build expensive tiny sheds ("houses") so they can go in to their back yard and "code in piece" - i.e. pursue their craft.
